summary: This informational RFC describes the design and architecture of Cisco's Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol. EIGRP is a distance vector routing protocol using an algorithm called DUAL, the Diffusing Update Algorithm.

eli5.summary: Routers tell neighbors how far away places are, and use a loop-avoiding method called DUAL to pick routes.

questions: how does the dual algorithm work
how does eigrp avoid routing loops
subtitle: A distance-vector routing protocol that uses DUAL to compute loop-free paths efficiently.

tldr.problem: Interior gateway routing protocols need to find the shortest paths to destinations while avoiding routing loops, especially when network topology changes. Traditional distance-vector protocols (like RIP) converge slowly and can create temporary loops.
tldr.mechanism: EIGRP uses the DUAL (Diffusing Update Algorithm), developed at SRI International, to compute loop-free paths guaranteed to be free of loops at every instant, even during topology changes. Only affected routers participate in recalculation, using the Feasibility Condition to verify loop freedom without waiting for global synchronization.
tldr.outcome: EIGRP provides fast convergence comparable to link-state protocols, with lower overhead and complexity. It scales well, coordinates updates efficiently, and allows routers to use Feasible Successors as immediate backup paths without topology changes.

sections.title: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol
sections.content:
EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol) is an interior gateway routing protocol designed and developed by Cisco Systems. It is a distance-vector routing protocol, meaning routers share information about distances (metrics) to destinations, which neighbors use to compute their own best paths. What makes EIGRP distinctive is its use of DUAL (Diffusing Update Algorithm), a sophisticated algorithm developed at SRI International that ensures loop-free routing at every instant, even while the network topology is changing.

Traditional distance-vector routing protocols (like RIP) can create temporary loops when a link fails or a metric changes. EIGRP avoids this by using the Feasibility Condition, a mathematical criterion that verifies loop freedom without waiting for all routers to reach agreement. Only routers affected by a topology change need to recalculate, which keeps overhead low and convergence fast.
sections.eli5: EIGRP is a system where routers tell their neighbors how far away different places are. It uses a special algorithm called DUAL that prevents messages from going in circles even when the network changes.

sections.title: Route States and the Feasibility Condition
sections.content:
In EIGRP, every route to a destination exists in one of two states: PASSIVE or ACTIVE. A route is in PASSIVE state when at least one neighbor provides the best-cost path and meets the Feasibility Condition, meaning the neighbor's reported distance to the destination is less than the router's own historical best distance (called the Feasible Distance). A PASSIVE route is usable and the router forwards traffic through its successor, the neighbor providing the best path.

When all neighbors providing the best path fail the Feasibility Condition (because their distances are no longer lower than the router's Feasible Distance), the route enters ACTIVE state. In ACTIVE state, the router cannot use any of its known paths and must query neighbors to find a new loop-free path. A Feasible Successor is a neighbor that meets the Feasibility Condition but is not currently the best path; these neighbors can become the successor immediately if the current path fails, without triggering an ACTIVE state computation.
sections.eli5: A route can be 'passive' (good to use) or 'active' (broken, need to find a new way). A neighbor is good to use if it is closer to the destination than you ever were before. That way, you never send traffic in circles.

sections.title: DUAL Algorithm and Query/Reply Coordination
sections.content:
When a topology change occurs, DUAL runs a diffusing computation to coordinate among affected routers and find a new loop-free path. If a route enters ACTIVE state, the router sends a QUERY message to all neighbors asking for their current distance to the destination. Neighbors respond with a REPLY message containing their distance; neighbors with Feasible Successors can reply immediately without entering ACTIVE state. Only neighbors that have no Feasible Successor will enter ACTIVE state and query their own neighbors, creating a diffusing wave of queries that grows across the affected part of the network and shrinks as routers reply.

The scope of the diffusion is controlled by the Feasibility Condition: unaffected routers are not required to participate in the recalculation. Once the router receives replies from all neighbors, it can exit ACTIVE state and select a new successor. If the reply process stalls (a router is stuck in ACTIVE state for too long), EIGRP sends SIA-QUERY and SIA-REPLY messages to determine whether a neighbor is still attempting to converge or has failed, and if needed, resets the neighbor relationship.
sections.eli5: When something breaks, the router asks neighbors 'how far are you from there?' Neighbors with a safe path reply right away. Others ask their neighbors, and so on. Once the router hears from everyone, it picks a new path.

sections.title: Packet Types and Reliable Transport
sections.content:
EIGRP uses five packet types to operate: HELLO (discovers and maintains neighbors), UPDATE (announces routing information), QUERY (requests alternate paths when entering ACTIVE state), REPLY (responds to queries), and REQUEST (asks for specific routing information). HELLO packets are sent unreliably and multicast to all neighbors; other packets are typically multicast on startup but then may be retransmitted as unicast if acknowledgment is not received. EIGRP implements its own reliable transport protocol to ensure ordered delivery: packets requiring acknowledgment are retransmitted up to 16 times over a 5-second period; if no acknowledgment is received after 16 retries, the neighbor relationship is reset.

EIGRP uses Type-Length-Value (TLV) encoding in packets to carry routing information in a flexible, backward-compatible format. The protocol supports both classic metrics (based on delay and bandwidth) and wide metrics (supporting higher-capacity links and additional attributes like jitter and energy). Split horizon is applied to prevent sending route information back to the neighbor from which it was learned, preventing certain types of loops.
sections.eli5: EIGRP packets are like postcards: HELLO says 'are you there?', UPDATE says 'this is how to reach there', QUERY says 'do you know how to reach there?', REPLY says 'yes, here is the way'. The router keeps trying to deliver important packets until they are received.

sections.title: Metrics and Path Computation
sections.content:
EIGRP computes a metric (cost) for each path by combining link characteristics using weighted parameters called K values. The classic metric formula uses K1 (bandwidth) and K3 (delay) primarily; by default, the metric is the inverse of the minimum bandwidth on the path plus the sum of delays. The metric is expressed as a 32-bit value in classic mode. EIGRP also defines wide metrics, a 64-bit encoding that supports high-speed links (10 Gbps and higher) and additional attributes like latency, jitter, and energy consumption. The Feasible Distance (FD) for a destination is the lowest total metric known since the route last entered PASSIVE state; the Computed Distance (CD) is the metric along a path through a particular neighbor.

When a router receives an UPDATE from a neighbor, it records the neighbor's Reported Distance (RD) to the destination and computes the total cost through that neighbor (CD = RD + link cost). If this CD is less than the current successor's cost, or if the neighbor has a lower RD than the current FD, the neighbor is a candidate as a Feasible Successor and may become the successor if the current path fails.
sections.eli5: Every link has a cost based on its speed and delay. The router adds up all the costs along a path to decide which path is best. If a neighbor is closer than you ever were, they can be a backup path.

sections.title: Deployment and Current Status
sections.content:
RFC 7868 is an Informational RFC that documents EIGRP as designed and deployed by Cisco Systems. It is not an Internet Standard, but it describes the complete design and architecture in detail. EIGRP has been widely deployed in enterprise networks for decades and remains a primary interior gateway protocol in Cisco-heavy environments. The protocol supports both IPv4 and IPv6, as well as other address families through its flexible multi-protocol architecture.

The RFC defines EIGRP's packet formats, the DUAL FSM (Finite State Machine) in detail, the reliable transport protocol, neighbor discovery procedures, and both classic and wide metric encodings. It also defines several IANA registries for future extensions without requiring RFC updates. Modern EIGRP implementations support features like named EIGRP (configuration by address family rather than process number) and support for modern attributes such as extended metrics and traffic engineering information.
sections.eli5: EIGRP is widely used in large networks. The RFC explains exactly how it works, so other companies can build their own versions and everyone's routers can talk to each other.
